name: Sinicized Miao
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: 康蔼德 (Andy Castro), 傅睿杰 (Royce Flaming), 罗有亮. 2012 [2022 typesetting]. 红河州苗语方言的发音与词汇比较 (Chinese edition of SIL ESR 2012-010).
sources.note: Same content in Chinese; 声调 (tone) sections only; no occurrence of 重音, 轻声 or 轻读.

sources.citation: Flaming, Royce & Andy Castro. 2021. Hmong Dialect Intelligibility in Southeastern Yunnan. Journal of Language Survey Reports 2021-045: 1-80. Dallas: SIL International.
sources.note: Most recent SIL work with Shuat and Hmong Sat data points; may contain updated phonological notes; open on sil.org but landing page id could not be resolved by automated download (an automated-access block on search pages).

sources.citation: Castro, Andy, Royce Flaming & Luo Youliang. 2012. A Phonological and Lexical Comparison of Western Miao Dialects in Honghe. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2012-010. Dallas: SIL International. 62 pp. (SIL archive 47764; PDF obtained via web.archive.org snapshot of the sil.org reapdata URL)
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2.3 'Sketch of Western Miao phonology' (p. 7): 'In all varieties of Western Miao, syllable structure is the same: onset + rhyme + tone.. C(C)V(V)(N), where tone is a suprasegmental feature that is expressed on the rhyme'; sec. 5.1.1 gives tone systems (7-10 lexical tones, breathiness; Hmong Sat shows a -t/-d phonetic tone switch not shared by Shuat); sec. 5.1.2.3 Shuat/Sat palatalised obstruents. Conclusions (p. 52) state explicitly that 'intonation patterns, tone sandhi, morphophonology' were not taken into account. The word 'stress' does not occur in the document (a full-text…

sources.citation: Castro, Andy & Gu Chaowen. 2010. Phonological innovation among Hmong dialects of Wenshan. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 3(1): 1-39. (primary Hmongb Shuat data point Yangliujing, Guangnan county; secondary Muyang, Funing county)
sources.note: Nothing. Treats Proto-Miao tone reflexes (Shuat retains an 8-tone system without the mergers of other Wenshan varieties), sec. 3.2.1 'Palatalised obstruents in Hmongb Shuat', nasal onsets; the word 'stress' does not occur (a full-text search for stress/accent count 0); no statement on accent, prominence or rhythm.

sources.citation: Schiering, René & Harry van der Hulst. 2010. Word accent systems in the languages of Asia. In van der Hulst, Goedemans & van Zanten (eds.), A Survey of Word Accentual Patterns in the Languages of the World, ch. 10 (pp. 509-599). Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. Sec. 7.3 Hmong-Mien.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, paywalled at the publisher
sources.note: Family-level only, no data for this language: 'Hmong-Mien is usually described as being exclusively tonal, but that does not imply that the languages in this family couldn't be accentual as well, cf. Chinese. Unfortunately, we did not have access to sources that would allow us to elaborate on this point.' (p. 596). Lists 'Hmong Shua' in the R. Gordon 2005 classification without accent data.

Chinese'): Castro et al. 2012:12 state it is 'based on Hmong Nzhuab spoken in Hekou county' (Green Hmong type, [hnj]).
